title: Understanding Essay Writing: Structure and Argument

pedagogy.rationale: Learners see a complete model essay plan and a model PEEL paragraph, take each part apart, practise choosing and ordering parts with feedback, and only then write their own thesis and paragraph. Writing builds on the MOE Grade 7 paragraph-writing work (topic sentences, kinds of paragraphs). Model evidence comes from a named practice school (Musu's school) and is labelled as made up; learners then plan before writing, write a conclusion and review a partner's paragraph against the PEEL questions.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Can write a paragraph with a topic sentence and supporting sentences (MOE Grade 7 paragraph writing).
Can tell a fact from an opinion in simple sentences.
Has discussed both sides of a school or community question in class.

misconceptions.description: Writes a topic or an announcement ('This essay is about gardens') instead of an arguable claim.
misconceptions.response: Ask: could a sensible person disagree with this sentence? If not, it is a topic or a fact, not a thesis.

misconceptions.description: Uses an opinion or a feeling ('everyone loves gardens') as if it were evidence.
misconceptions.response: Evidence must be something the reader can check or picture: an example, a fact with a source, or a real experience.

misconceptions.description: Repeats the claim as its own reason ('gardens are good because they are good').
misconceptions.response: A reason answers 'why?' with new information. Say what the garden does, not just that it is good.

misconceptions.description: Gives true but unrelated evidence that does not support the reason in that paragraph.
misconceptions.response: Read the reason and the evidence together: does the evidence prove this reason, or something else?

misconceptions.description: Thinks mentioning the other side weakens an essay, so never answers objections.
misconceptions.response: Answering the strongest objection shows the reader you have thought it through, and makes your claim harder to reject.

misconceptions.description: Adds a brand-new reason in the conclusion.
misconceptions.response: The conclusion restates the thesis in new words and sums up the reasons already argued; new reasons belong in a body paragraph.

scenes.title: Why write an argument?
scenes.learnerAction: Read the situation and think about how you would convince the meeting.

content.body:
At a PTA meeting, parents and teachers disagree: should the school use its empty land for a **school garden**? Some people speak well, but a week later nobody remembers exactly what they said.

A written argument lasts. An **argumentative essay** puts your claim, your reasons and your evidence in an order a reader can follow, so they can judge your argument and maybe agree with you. Today you will learn that order and use it.

accessibility.textAlternative: Introduction: a PTA meeting disagrees about a school garden. A written argumentative essay organizes a claim, reasons and evidence so a reader can follow and judge it.

scenes.title: Warm-up: paragraphs and facts
scenes.learnerAction: Answer two questions from your paragraph-writing lessons and read the feedback.

content.body: Essays are built from paragraphs. Check what you remember. These answers are not marked.

items.prompt: What does a topic sentence do?

options.text: It tells the main idea of the paragraph
options.feedback: Yes. The topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about, usually at the start.

options.text: It gives the last small detail
options.feedback: Details support the main idea. The topic sentence states the main idea itself, usually first.

options.text: It always asks the reader a question
options.feedback: A question can be a hook, but a topic sentence states the paragraph's main idea.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a fact, not an opinion?

options.text: School gardens are the best thing a school can have.
options.feedback: 'The best' is a judgement, so this is an opinion. People could disagree.

options.text: Cassava leaves are grown and eaten in many parts of Liberia.
options.feedback: Yes. This can be checked, so it is a fact.

options.text: Everyone loves working in the garden.
options.feedback: This is an opinion about how people feel, and it is not true of everyone.

hints: A fact can be checked; an opinion is what someone thinks or feels.

feedback.onSuccess: You already know two building blocks of an essay.
feedback.onStruggle: That is fine. The next scenes show where topic sentences and facts fit in an essay.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two warm-up questions: what a topic sentence does, and which sentence is a fact. Each answer shows written feedback.

scenes.title: The three parts of an argumentative essay
scenes.learnerAction: Study the essay diagram and the job of each part.

content.body:
An argumentative essay has three parts, and each part has a job.

The **introduction** catches the reader's attention with a hook, gives a little background, and ends with the **thesis statement**: your claim and the main reasons for it.

Each **body paragraph** argues one reason. It starts with a **topic sentence**, then gives evidence and explains it. A strong essay also uses one paragraph to answer the other side.

The **conclusion** restates the thesis in new words, sums up the reasons, and ends with a final thought or a call to action. It does not add new reasons.
keyPoints: Introduction: hook, background, thesis statement.
Body: one reason per paragraph, each with a topic sentence, evidence and explanation.
Conclusion: restate, sum up, final thought. No new reasons.

media.description: An essay drawn as three stacked blocks: introduction (hook, background, thesis), body paragraphs (topic sentence, evidence, explanation; one answers the other side), conclusion (restate, sum up, final thought).
media.altText: Essay structure: introduction with hook, background and thesis; body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, evidence and explanation, one answering the other side; conclusion that restates, sums up and ends with a final thought.

accessibility.textAlternative: The three parts of an argumentative essay and the job of each: introduction with thesis, body paragraphs with topic sentences and evidence, and a conclusion that adds no new reasons.

scenes.title: Take apart a model essay plan
scenes.learnerAction: Open each part of the model essay plan in order.

content.body: Here is a plan for the essay **Every school in Liberia should have a school garden**. Open each part to see what the writer put there and why.

steps.label: Introduction: hook
steps.description: Imagine eating fresh greens at lunch that you and your classmates grew yourselves. (A picture the reader can imagine pulls them in.)

steps.label: Introduction: thesis statement
steps.description: Every school in Liberia should have a school garden because gardens teach useful farming and science skills and give schools fresh food for learners. (Claim + two reasons.)

steps.label: Body paragraph 1: first reason
steps.description: Topic sentence: A school garden turns science and agriculture lessons into real work. The paragraph then gives evidence and explains it.

steps.label: Body paragraph 2: second reason
steps.description: Topic sentence: A garden can add fresh vegetables to school meals. Evidence and explanation follow.

steps.label: Body paragraph 3: the other side
steps.description: Some people say gardens take time away from lessons. But garden work can be part of science and agriculture lessons, done in short weekly sessions. (Objection, then answer.)

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.description: School gardens build skills and feed learners. Every school with land should start one this year. (Restate, sum up, call to action; no new reasons.)

hints: Notice that each body paragraph matches one reason from the thesis.

accessibility.textAlternative: Six text steps of a model plan for 'Every school in Liberia should have a school garden': hook, thesis, two reason paragraphs, an answer to the other side, and a conclusion.

scenes.title: Guided practice: what makes a strong thesis
scenes.learnerAction: Choose the strongest thesis in each question and read why.

content.body:
A strong thesis statement is a **claim**: a sentence a sensible person could disagree with. It is specific, and it names the reasons the essay will argue.

A topic ('school gardens'), a plain fact ('some schools have gardens') or an announcement ('I will write about gardens') is not a thesis, because there is nothing to argue.
keyPoints: Claim: could someone disagree?
Specific: says exactly what should happen.
Reasons: names why, so the reader knows what is coming.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest thesis statement?

options.text: School gardens.
options.feedback: This is only a topic. It does not say what you think about gardens.

options.text: Some schools in Liberia have gardens.
options.feedback: This is a fact. Nobody would argue about it, so there is nothing to prove.

options.text: Every school in Liberia should have a school garden because gardens teach farming skills and provide fresh food.
options.feedback: Yes. It is a claim someone could disagree with, it is specific, and it names two reasons.

options.text: I will write about gardens in this essay.
options.feedback: This announces the topic but makes no claim.

items.prompt: Which sentence could a sensible person disagree with?

options.text: Monrovia is the capital of Liberia.
options.feedback: This is a fact that can be checked. It cannot be argued.

options.text: Students should have 30 minutes of reading time every school day because it builds vocabulary and confidence.
options.feedback: Yes. Some people might say the time is needed for other subjects, so this claim can be argued.

options.text: Many students go to school.
options.feedback: This is a general fact, not a claim to argue.

hints: Ask: could a sensible person disagree with this sentence?

feedback.onSuccess: You can tell a claim from a topic or a fact.
feedback.onStruggle: Look for the word 'should' or a clear opinion, plus a reason.

accessibility.textAlternative: What makes a strong thesis, then two questions: choose the strongest thesis and choose the sentence someone could disagree with, each with written feedback.

scenes.title: Build a body paragraph with PEEL
scenes.learnerAction: Open each PEEL sentence of the model paragraph in order.

content.body: A strong body paragraph follows **PEEL**: **P**oint, **E**vidence, **E**xplain, **L**ink. Open each step to build the first body paragraph of the garden essay.

steps.label: P: Point (topic sentence)
steps.description: A school garden turns science and agriculture lessons into real work.

steps.label: E: Evidence
steps.description: For example, in Musu's school garden, learners measure the beds, test which soil holds water best and record how fast each plant grows.

steps.label: E: Explain
steps.description: This shows that the garden makes learners practise measuring, testing and recording: skills they need in science class and on a family farm.

steps.label: L: Link
steps.description: So a garden makes lessons more useful, which is one reason every school should have one.

media.description: Four stacked boxes labelled Point, Evidence, Explain and Link, each holding one sentence of the model garden paragraph, with arrows showing how each sentence leads to the next.
media.altText: PEEL paragraph: Point (a garden turns lessons into real work), Evidence (learners measure beds, test soil, record growth), Explain (they practise science and farming skills), Link (so every school should have a garden).

hints: The Explain sentence answers: so what? How does this evidence prove the point?

accessibility.textAlternative: A model PEEL paragraph in four text steps: point, evidence, explanation and link, about how a garden turns lessons into real work.

scenes.title: Choosing strong evidence
scenes.learnerAction: Learn four kinds of evidence and the questions that test them.

content.body:
Evidence is what makes a reader believe your reason. Four kinds are useful in school essays: **facts and figures** from a source you can name, **examples** of real events, the words of an **expert** (such as a teacher, nurse or agriculture officer), and your own **experience**.

Before you use evidence, test it with four questions. Never make up a fact or a number: if you use a figure, say where it comes from.

In this lesson, examples about **Musu's school** are made-up practice examples. They show what good evidence looks like, but they are not facts. In your own writing, use only evidence that is real.
keyPoints: Is it true, and can the reader check it?
Is it relevant: does it prove this reason?
Is it specific: who, what, where, when?
Where does it come from?

media.description: Four evidence cards (facts and figures, examples, expert words, experience) passing through a four-question test: true, relevant, specific, source.

scenes.title: Watch out: weak evidence and weak reasons
scenes.learnerAction: Choose the best answer to each question and read why.

content.body: Writers often fall into these traps. Choose an answer for each question, then read the explanation.

items.prompt: Reason: a garden can add fresh vegetables to school meals. Which evidence supports this reason best? (Musu's school is the made-up practice school from this lesson.)

options.text: Gardens look beautiful when the flowers bloom.
options.feedback: This may be true, but it is about beauty, not school meals. It does not prove this reason.

options.text: At Musu's school, the agriculture club's greens and pepper were used in school lunches for a week last term.
options.feedback: Yes. It is specific and it proves this exact reason: the garden added vegetables to school meals. In your own essay, use a real example like this from your school or community.

options.text: Gardens are good, and everyone knows it.
options.feedback: This is an opinion repeated, not evidence. The reader cannot check it.

options.text: Many countries have gardens.
options.feedback: This is too vague and says nothing about school meals.

items.prompt: Musa writes: 'School gardens are good because they are good for schools.' What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing. It is a strong argument.
options.feedback: Look again: the reason only repeats the claim. It never says what the garden does.

options.text: It repeats the claim instead of giving a real reason.
options.feedback: Yes. A reason answers 'why?' with new information, such as 'because gardens give schools fresh food'.

options.text: The sentence is too long.
options.feedback: Length is not the problem. The reason says nothing new.

items.prompt: Why should an argumentative essay mention the other side?

options.text: To show the writer has changed their mind.
options.feedback: The writer keeps their claim. They mention the other side in order to answer it.

options.text: To answer a likely objection, which makes the argument stronger.
options.feedback: Yes. Answering the strongest objection shows you have thought it through.

options.text: To make the essay longer.
options.feedback: Length is not the goal. Answering an objection makes the argument harder to reject.

hints: Read the reason and the evidence together. Does the evidence prove this reason?

feedback.onSuccess: You can spot weak evidence and weak reasons.
feedback.onStruggle: Go back to the evidence test questions and try again.

accessibility.textAlternative: Three questions: choose the evidence that best supports a reason, spot a reason that repeats the claim, and explain why essays answer the other side.

scenes.title: Put a paragraph in PEEL order
scenes.learnerAction: Read the four sentences and write their letters in PEEL order.

content.body: These four sentences make one body paragraph, but they are mixed up. Put them in PEEL order: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
keyPoints: A. So when learners grow food at school, everyone eats better, which is why every school needs a garden.
B. Fresh vegetables from a school garden can make school meals healthier.
C. This shows that the garden gives the kitchen food it would otherwise have to buy or go without.
D. For example, at Musu's school the garden's greens and pepper were used in lunch for a whole week last term.

interaction.prompt: Put the four sentences in PEEL order.
elements: A: Link sentence about everyone eating better
C: Explanation about food for the kitchen
D: Evidence about a week of lunches

fallback.content: Write the four letters in PEEL order (for example: X, X, X, X), then say which letter is the topic sentence.

scenes.expectedObservation: B, D, C, A. B is the topic sentence (Point).
hints: The Point is the topic sentence: it states the reason.
The Link connects back to the thesis, so it comes last.

feedback.onSuccess: You can see the job of each sentence.
feedback.onStruggle: Find the topic sentence first, then the sentence that starts with 'For example'.

scenes.title: Plan before you write
scenes.learnerAction: Choose a topic, brainstorm reasons, then plan your claim, two reasons and real evidence.

content.body: Good writers plan first. Choose one topic and decide what you think. Then **brainstorm**: for two minutes, list every reason you can think of without judging them. Next, choose your **two strongest** reasons. For each one, write one piece of **real** evidence and where it comes from: something you saw, a fact you can check, or the words of someone you can name. If you cannot find real evidence for a reason, choose a different reason.
keyPoints: Topic 1: Every community should have a public library.
Topic 2: Schools should start each day with 20 minutes of reading.
Topic 3: Learners should help keep their school compound clean every week.
Plan: claim → reason 1 + evidence → reason 2 + evidence.

prompts.prompt: Brainstorm: list at least four reasons for your claim, one per line.
Your plan: write your claim, then your two strongest reasons, each with one piece of real evidence and where it comes from.

scenes.expectedObservation: Brainstorm lists several different reasons. The plan states an arguable claim, two reasons that answer 'why?', and for each a specific, checkable piece of evidence with its source (an observation, a checkable fact or a named person). Watch for Musu's school examples copied as evidence, opinions used as evidence, and reasons that repeat the claim.
hints: Write fast while you brainstorm; choose later.
Ask of each piece of evidence: is it true, and where does it come from?

feedback.onSuccess: Your plan gives every paragraph a job before you write it.
feedback.onStruggle: Start with your claim, then finish the sentence 'because …' twice.

accessibility.textAlternative: Choose one of three topics, brainstorm at least four reasons, then write a plan: a claim and two reasons, each with real evidence and its source. Two text boxes.

scenes.title: Write your own thesis and PEEL paragraph
scenes.learnerAction: Use your plan to write a thesis and one PEEL body paragraph.

content.body: Now write, using your plan. Use only real evidence: an example you know, a fact you can check, or your own experience. Do not borrow Musu's school examples: they are made up. Your teacher reads this writing; it is not marked by this lesson.
keyPoints: Point: your first reason, as a topic sentence.
Evidence: one real, specific example or fact from your plan.
Explain: how the evidence proves the point.
Link: back to your claim.

prompts.prompt: Write the thesis statement from your plan: your claim and two reasons.
Write one body paragraph for your first reason using PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

scenes.expectedObservation: Thesis is an arguable claim that names two reasons. Paragraph opens with a topic sentence matching reason one, gives specific true evidence, explains how it supports the point, and links back to the claim.
hints: Start your thesis with your claim, then use 'because' to add two reasons.
Begin your paragraph with your first reason as the topic sentence.

feedback.onSuccess: You have written the core of an argumentative essay.
feedback.onStruggle: Use the PEEL model paragraph as a guide and write one sentence for each letter.

scenes.title: Write a conclusion
scenes.learnerAction: Write a conclusion for the school-garden essay.

content.body: Go back to the model plan for **Every school in Liberia should have a school garden**. Its body paragraphs argued two reasons (gardens teach farming and science skills, and they add fresh food to school meals) and answered one objection (garden work takes time from lessons). Write a conclusion of three or four sentences that does the three jobs of a conclusion. Do not copy the model plan's conclusion, and do not add a new reason.
keyPoints: Restate the thesis in new words.
Sum up the two reasons (and, if you like, the answer to the other side).
End with a final thought or a call to action.
Check: no new reasons.

prompts.prompt: Write your conclusion for the school-garden essay (three or four sentences).

scenes.expectedObservation: Restates the claim without copying the thesis, sums up both reasons (skills; fresh food), ends with a final thought or call to action, and adds no new reason (for example, not 'gardens also make the compound beautiful').
hints: Begin with a phrase such as 'For these reasons' or 'In short'.
Read each sentence: does it give a reason the body did not argue? If so, remove it.

feedback.onSuccess: Your conclusion closes the argument without opening a new one.
feedback.onStruggle: Write one sentence for each of the three jobs.

accessibility.textAlternative: Write a three- or four-sentence conclusion for the school-garden essay: restate the thesis in new words, sum up its two reasons, end with a final thought, and add no new reason.

scenes.title: Peer review: one strength, one next step
scenes.learnerAction: Swap paragraphs with a partner, check them against four questions, then write one strength and one next step.

content.body: Swap your PEEL paragraph with a partner and read it twice. Check it against the four questions below, then give honest, kind feedback: one **strength** and one **next step**. Talk about the writing, not the writer. If you are working alone, review your own paragraph the same way.
keyPoints: Point: does the topic sentence state a clear reason that matches the thesis?
Evidence: is it real and specific, and is its source named?
Explain: does a sentence show how the evidence proves the point?
Link: does the last sentence connect back to the claim?
Sentence starters: 'One strength is … because …' and 'Next time, try …'

prompts.prompt: Write one strength of the paragraph you reviewed. Name the question it meets and quote the words that show it.
Write one next step: name a question the paragraph does not yet meet and suggest one change.

scenes.expectedObservation: Feedback names a specific question and points to words in the paragraph; the next step is one concrete change (for example 'say where this figure comes from'). Watch for vague praise ('good job'), comments about the writer instead of the writing, and accepting made-up evidence as real.
hints: Quote the exact words that meet, or miss, a question.
A next step says what to change, not just that something is wrong.

feedback.onSuccess: Specific feedback helps a writer know exactly what to keep and what to change.
feedback.onStruggle: Choose one question from the list and answer it about the paragraph.

accessibility.textAlternative: Swap PEEL paragraphs with a partner (or review your own), check the paragraph against four questions on point, evidence, explanation and link, then write one strength and one next step.

scenes.title: Key ideas to remember
scenes.learnerAction: Read the key ideas before the exit ticket.

content.body: Before the exit ticket, review the big ideas of this lesson.
keyPoints: An essay has an introduction (ending with the thesis), body paragraphs and a conclusion.
A thesis is a claim someone could disagree with, plus the reasons you will argue.
Each body paragraph follows PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
Strong evidence is true, relevant and specific, and you can say where it comes from.
Plan before you write: claim, two reasons, and real evidence for each.
Answer the other side; do not add new reasons in the conclusion.
